title: The Tide Takes Inventory
subtitle: A Lanternweald continuation
content:
The morning after the festival, I found the welcome sign floating face down in the cove.

At first, I thought someone had played a joke.

Maui had been very proud of that sign. It was carved from a piece of driftwood with a curve like a smile, painted in a blue that matched the thread holding my brass key. WELCOME TO TIDEGLASS COVE, it said. SAFE LANDING AT ALL TIDES, it said beneath.

The second line had been his idea.

I waded in far enough to reach the sign. The water was cold. A small crab took offense to my ankle. I took offense to the crab.

By the time I dragged the sign onto the sand, Maui had appeared with a spear in one hand and the expression of a man who had expected to fight something large.

"Who's attacking?"

"The ocean."

He looked at the sign.

"The ocean has terrible manners."

"The ocean also appears to have won."

Maui planted the spear in the sand. His tattoos shifted as he crouched beside the wood.

"Probably a wave."

"Probably several." I pointed toward the dock.

The outermost post leaned at an angle that had not been there yesterday. Beyond it, the new landing boards sat crooked above the tide. One rope had worn almost through where it passed around the mooring ring.

Maui's smile disappeared.

"Nobody's hurt," he said.

"Not yet."

He stood. "I'll fix it."

I caught the edge of his wrist before he could take three long heroic strides into the water.

"That's not the same as checking whether it's safe."

"I built it."

"I know. That's why I'm asking you to look."

He stared down at my hand. I let go. His pride had begun to rise, hot and quick, but so had his worry.

He looked at the dock again.

"All right," he said, more quietly. "We look."

We fetched Fen Arlow, the canal steward, who arrived carrying a measuring stick and an expression that suggested he had already heard about our sign.

"Safe at all tides," he read.

"I would like to submit an amendment," I said.

Fen stepped onto the first plank, pressed it with the heel of his boot, and stepped back.

"Good instinct. The outer post is seated in sand, not stone. The channel shifts after the first hard autumn tide."

Maui folded his arms. "It held through the festival."

"Your festival happened at low tide."

"It was a very successful festival."

"Congratulations. The sea doesn't attend council meetings."

I nearly smiled. Maui did not.

Fen showed us the dark line water had left against the rocks. It was well above the welcome sign's promised safe level.

"We need a new post," Fen said. "Maybe two. And until then, that landing is closed."

Maui picked up the sign. "I can replace the whole thing before lunch."

"With what timber?" Fen asked.

"The trees."

"Which trees?"

"The—" Maui gestured toward the hillside. "Trees."

"Somebody owns those. Somebody else planted the young ones to stop the bank from sliding. You cannot solve one problem by creating another."

Maui's face did something complicated.

I recognized the moment. He was being told that strength was not enough, and he was struggling not to hear it as proof that he was not enough.

"I'll find the wood," he said.

Fen nodded. "Good. Get permission. Bring it to the yard. We'll test it."

That afternoon the three of us walked the shoreline with Tamsin Vale, the lanternwright, who had once helped maintain the cove steps. Her tool bag clinked when she moved.

"How did your sign end up in the water?" she asked.

"Poor leadership," I said.

Maui shot me a look.

"Not just yours," I added. "Mine too. I approved the wording."

Tamsin touched the scraped paint with a thumbnail. "Then you can both approve the correction."

We spent an hour marking tide heights on the stone steps. Another hour counting what the cove actually had: four sound ropes, one damaged mooring ring, a stack of timber too narrow for the outer rail, two usable lantern brackets and a remarkably stubborn crab that refused to vacate the supply basket.

By sunset, my notebook held three pages of disappointing facts.

Maui stood over my shoulder.

"I thought this place would be easier."

"Because it's magical?"

"Because it wanted us here."

I closed the notebook. "A place can welcome us and still need maintenance."

He sat beside me on the step. The wind lifted his hair from his shoulders. Salt had dried along one edge of his tattooed arm.

"I wanted to build you somewhere you could come back to," he said.

"You did."

"It broke."

"The dock broke. The choice didn't."

He watched the dark water.

I leaned my shoulder against his. For once, he did not make a speech about being impressive. He leaned back.

"People keep asking you what the doors mean," he said. "Who you'll visit. How often you'll come back."

"People can be curious. It doesn't mean they get to vote."

"I know." He hesitated. "I'm trying to remember what you said. About loving people without locking them up."

I touched the little brass key at my throat. "I meant it."

"So did I. About wanting to try, even when the questions are stupid."

"Do you have one?"

He took a breath.

"If somebody else builds you something that doesn't break, would you stop wanting to come here?"

It hurt, because I could hear how carefully he had made the question small.

"Maui." I turned toward him. "I want to come here because this is home. Not because the dock is perfect, and not because somebody won me at a festival."

He looked at me.

"And if I love someone else someday, I'm still responsible for what I promise you. I don't get to leave you guessing. Neither do you."

He let that settle.

"All right."

"All right?"

"I think I can live with a promise that involves actual work."

"Revolutionary."

He grinned, finally.

Then he leaned down to kiss me, stopped close enough for his breath to warm my cheek, and waited.

"Yes," I whispered.

His lips were soft despite every boast he'd ever made about them. He smelled like salt and the wood shavings caught in his clothes. The first kiss of the evening became a second when I tugged lightly at his hand.

Somewhere above us, the first lantern came on.

We stayed until it was too dark to count posts.

The next morning, before the bakery opened, we took the welcome sign to the workshop. Tamsin sanded away the damaged line while I painted new letters in careful white strokes.

WELCOME TO TIDEGLASS COVE.

CHECK THE TIDE CHART BEFORE LANDING.

Maui regarded the result.

"Less dramatic."

"More accurate."

"I could add a sea monster."

"On the safety sign?"

"Only a small one."

I handed him the brush.

He painted a tiny crab at the bottom instead.

I liked it better that way.

For the first time, the sign told the truth. And when we carried it back down to the shore, nobody had to pretend that made the water harmless.
